extraction_notes.note: Proofs are written as \proof ... \endproof (plain TeX), which latex_facts does not report as proof facts; each was emitted as a prose proof spanning \proof to \endproof with a named proves edge (confidence 0.9).

Theorem 4.5's source contains stray Hebrew vowel marks inside \tilde{N}_{i,k}, copied verbatim.
finalize warns that DP14 introduces symbols in separate sentences; the split it sees is the 'e.g.' abbreviation inside one sentence, so DP14 was kept whole (nodes never split a sentence).

Euler's transformation (4.18) is named as a result, so it was retyped theorem/external; Ghosh's density (4.17) and the Gauss-theorem limit (4.20) are cited formulas not named as results and stay equations (Ghosh's with origin external).

nodes.statement: However, our asymptotic analysis motivates a conjecture that the optimal sample size in the first stage of both procedures grows logarithmically in the number of populations, and with this optimal choice the multiplicative factor approaches one and the two procedures may be asymptotically equivalent.

nodes.name: I.i.d. sequence X_m with c.d.f. F
nodes.statement: Let $\{X_m;m=1,2,\ldots\}$ be an infinite sequence of identically independently distributed (i.i.d) continuous random-variables (r.v's) with cumulative distribution function (c.d.f) $F$ such that $F(-\infty)=0$ and $\underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim} F(x) =1$.

nodes.name: Partition s_k^(t) of {1,..,k} into T sub-groups
nodes.statement: Let $T\in\mathbb{N}$ and for each $k>T$ let $1=:s_k^{(0)} < s_k^{(1)}<\ldots<s_k^{(T-1)}<s_k^{(T)}:=k$ be an increasing integer sequence defining a partition of $\{1,..,k\}$ into $T$ sub-groups.

nodes.name: Partial maxima M_k^(t)
nodes.statement: Define the partial maxima of $\{X_m;m=1,\ldots,k\}$ with respect to this partition by $M_k^{(t)}:=\max\{X_j;s_k^{(t-1)}+1\leq j\leq s_k^{(t)}\}$, $t\in\mathcal{T}:=\{1,\ldots,T\}$.

nodes.name: Broad-sense convergence of the group sizes delta_k^(t)
nodes.statement: With regard to this sequence of partitions assume that for each $t\in\mathcal{T}$ the difference $\delta_k^{(t)} :=s_k^{(t)}-s_k^{(t-1)}$ converges in the broad sense, i.e. there exist $\delta^{(t)}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ such that $\delta_k^{(t)} \overset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \delta^{(t)}$.

nodes.name: Max-stable distribution (normalizing constants a_k, b_k)
nodes.statement: Moreover, let $F$ be max-stable in the sense that it is associated with an extreme value distribution, i.e. there are two sequences of normalizing constants $\{a_k\}$ and $\{b_k\}$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item There exists $K\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a_k>0$ for any $k>K$. \item $\{a_k\}$ is weakly-monotonic. \item $a_k\big(\underset{j=1,\ldots,k}{\max} X_j-b_k\big) \xrightarrow {\mathcal{L}}Y$ where the notation $\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}$ denotes convergence in law of r.v's and $Y\sim F_Y$ is a continuous r.v, i.e. its c.d.f $F_Y$ is characterized by Fisher-Tippet-Gnedenko's theorem. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: F is max-stable when eventually positive, weakly monotone constants $a_k,b_k$ give $a_k(\max_{j\le k}X_j-b_k)\to Y$ in law, $Y$ continuous.

nodes.name: Limit of linear combinations of partial maxima (a_infinity > 0)
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a max-stable distribution associated with sequences $\{a_k\}, \{b_k\}$ such that $a_\infty\in(0,\infty]$. For each $t\in\mathcal{T}_1$, let $M_t$ be a random variable distributed as the maximum of $\delta^{(t)}$ i.i.d. random variables with c.d.f. $F$, i.e. $M_t \sim F^{\delta^{(t)}}$ and for each $t\in\mathcal{T}_2$, let $Y_t\sim F_Y$ such that $\{M_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_1\}\cup\{Y_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_2\}$ is a set of independent r.v's. Then: \begin{equation} L=F_V(L^*). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Convergence of c.d.f. values under convergence in law
nodes.statement: If $V$ is a finite r.v and $V_1,V_2\ldots$ are r.v's such that \begin{enumerate} \item $V_k\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}V$. \item $F_V$ is continuous on $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. \item $\{x_k;k\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is a deterministic sequence such that $x_k\rightarrow\bar{x}$ where $\bar{x}\in\mathcal{C}\cup\{-\infty,\infty\}$ . \end{enumerate} Then $F_{V_k}(x_k)\xrightarrow[k\rightarrow\infty]{} F_V(\bar{x})$.

nodes.statement: Let $s \in \mathbb{N}$. If $\forall k\in\mathbb{N}$, $Z_k^{(1)},\ldots,Z_k^{(s)}$ are independent r.v's such that $Z_k^{(i)}\xrightarrow[k\rightarrow\infty]{\mathcal{L}}Z_i, \: \forall i=1,\ldots,s$, then \begin{equation} Z_k^{(1)}+\ldots +Z_k^{(s)}\xrightarrow[k\rightarrow\infty]{\mathcal{L}}Z_1+\ldots+Z_s \end{equation} where $Z_1,\ldots,Z_s$ are independent r.v's.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma:convergence_sum} is obtained by a straightforward application of the multivariate continuous mapping theorem for the vector $(Z_k^{(1)},\ldots,Z_k^{(s)})$, noticing that due to independence we have $(Z_k^{(1)},\ldots,Z_k^{(s)})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_s)$.
nodes.statement_short: Multivariate continuous mapping theorem applied to the jointly converging independent vector.

nodes.statement: L &= \lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}\leq\xi_k\big) \nonumber \\ &=\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}\leq\xi_k\big) \nonumber \\ &= \lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\frac{\alpha_t}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}(M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\leq\xi_k-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t b_{\delta_k^{(t)}}\big) .

nodes.name: Lemma 2 gives convergence of the sum to V
nodes.statement: Therefore, Lemma \ref{lemma:convergence_sum} implies that \begin{equation} \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\frac{\alpha_t}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}(M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t M_t+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\frac{\alpha_t}{a_\infty} Y_t=V \end{equation} where $\{M_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_1\}\cup\{Y_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_2\}$ is a set of independent r.v's.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 gives convergence of the sum to V

nodes.name: Sum of both parts converges to V

nodes.label: eq:sum_two_parts

nodes.name: Case some alpha_t/a_inf = 0: Slutsky
nodes.statement: At this stage, assume that $\exists t'\in\mathcal{T}_2$ for which $\frac{\alpha_{t'}}{a_\infty}=0$. The LHS of eq. (\ref{eq:sum_two_parts}) can be represented as the sum of two finite sums $\mathcal{S}_1+\mathcal{S}_2$, where $\mathcal{S}_1$ includes all summands that converge in law to zero and $\mathcal{S}_2$ includes all other summands. Recalling that convergence in law to a constant implies convergence in probability, then each of the summands in $\mathcal{S}_1$ converges in probability to zero, and since the number of summands is finite, $\mathcal{S}_1 \overset{\mathbb{P}}{\rightarrow} 0$ . Similarly, by the arguments used under the simplifying assumption that $\frac{\alpha_t}{a_\infty}\neq0,\forall t\in\mathcal{T}_2$, $\mathcal{S}_2 \overset{\mathbb{L}}{\rightarrow} V$. Therefore, by Slutsky's Lemma (see Chapter $6$ in \cite{ferguson1996course}), the total sum converges in law to $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Split off the summands converging to zero and conclude convergence to $V$ by Slutsky's lemma.

nodes.name: V is continuous
nodes.statement: The distribution of $Y$ is characterized by Fisher-Tippet-Gnedenko's Theorem hence $Y$ is a continuous r.v. In addition, $M_t$ is distributed like a maximum of a finite number of i.i.d continuous r.v's, and is a continuous r.v. Therefore, deduce that $V$ is a finite sum of independent continuous r.v's and hence it is a continuous r.v.
nodes.statement_short: V is continuous

nodes.statement: Finally, since $L^*$ exists in the broad sense, the needed result follows directly from Lemma \ref{lemma:convergence_law}.

nodes.statement: L &= \lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}\leq\xi_k\big) \nonumber \\ &= \mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t M_k^{(t)}\leq\xi_k\big) \nonumber \\ &= \lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t\frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\leq a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}\big(\xi_k-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_tb_{\delta_k^{(t)}}\big)\Big) .

nodes.name: Limits in law of each scaled summand
nodes.statement: By similar arguments as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:sum_max_a_k_positive}, \begin{enumerate} \item $\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}0$ , $\forall t\in\mathcal{T}_1$. \item $\alpha_t \frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\alpha_t \lambda_tY_t$, $\forall t\in\mathcal{T}_2$. \item For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $M_k^{(1)},\ldots,M_k^{(T)}$ are independent r.v's. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Limits in law of each scaled summand

nodes.name: Item 1: finite groups vanish in law
nodes.statement: $\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}0$ , $\forall t\in\mathcal{T}_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Item 1: finite groups vanish in law

nodes.name: Item 2: infinite groups converge to alpha_t lambda_t Y_t
nodes.statement: $\alpha_t \frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\alpha_t \lambda_tY_t$, $\forall t\in\mathcal{T}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Item 2: infinite groups converge to alpha_t lambda_t Y_t

nodes.name: Item 3: independence
nodes.statement: For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $M_k^{(1)},\ldots,M_k^{(T)}$ are independent r.v's.
nodes.statement_short: Item 3: independence

nodes.name: Lemma 2: infinite groups converge to V
nodes.statement: Since all the preconditions of Lemma \ref{lemma:convergence_sum} are satisfied, deduce that \begin{equation} \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t \frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t \lambda_t Y_t=V\ \ . \end{equation} where $\{Y_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_1\}$ are independent r.v's.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2: infinite groups converge to V

nodes.name: Infinite-group sum converges to V
nodes.statement: \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t \frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t \lambda_t Y_t=V\ \ .

nodes.name: Finite groups vanish in probability
nodes.statement: On the other hand, because convergence in law to a constant implies convergence in probability, \begin{equation} \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow} 0 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Finite groups vanish in probability

nodes.name: Finite-group sum tends to 0 in probability
nodes.statement: \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow} 0 .

nodes.name: Slutsky: total sum converges to V
nodes.statement: Thus, Slutsky's Lemma can be applied to obtain the following limit: \begin{equation} \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t\frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\overset{\mathcal{L}}{\longrightarrow} 0+V=V . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Slutsky: total sum converges to V

nodes.name: Total sum converges to V
nodes.statement: \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_1}\alpha_t a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}M_k^{(t)}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\alpha_t\frac{a_{\delta^{t^*}_k}}{a_{\delta_k^{(t)}}} a_{\delta_k^{(t)}} (M_k^{(t)}-b_{\delta_k^{(t)}})\overset{\mathcal{L}}{\longrightarrow} 0+V=V .

nodes.name: V is continuous
nodes.statement: Fisher-Tippet-Gnedenko's Theorem implies that $\{Y_t;t\in\mathcal{T}_1\}$ are continuous r.v's. Therefore, $V$ is a finite sum of finite continuous independent r.v's, so it is also a finite continuous r.v.
nodes.statement_short: V is continuous

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Finally, since $L^*$ exists in the broad sense, Lemma \ref{lemma:convergence_law} implies the needed result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 1

nodes.name: Homoscedastic Gaussian populations X_ij ~ N(theta_i, sigma^2)
nodes.statement: Let $X_{ij}\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma^2);i=1,\ldots,k, \: j=1,\ldots,N$ be independent univariate Gaussian r.v's with known variance $\sigma^2>0$ and unknown means $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k)\in\mathbb{R}^k$.

nodes.name: Selecting the s populations with the largest means
nodes.statement: The task is to find the $1\leq s\leq \lfloor \frac{k}{2}\rfloor$ populations with the largest means.

nodes.name: Natural selection by empirical means
nodes.statement: An intuitive procedure for this purpose is to compute the empirical means $\bar{X}_i:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^NX_{ij}, \: \forall i=1,\ldots,k$ and select the $s$ populations associated with the highest values.
output: the $s$ populations associated with the highest values
nodes.statement_short: Compute each population's empirical mean $\bar X_i$ and select the $s$ populations with the largest ones.

nodes.name: Compute the empirical means
nodes.statement: compute the empirical means $\bar{X}_i:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^NX_{ij}, \: \forall i=1,\ldots,k$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\bar X_i=\frac1N\sum_jX_{ij}$ for each population.

nodes.name: Select the s largest means
nodes.statement: select the $s$ populations associated with the highest values
nodes.statement_short: Select the s largest means

nodes.name: Minimal common sample size N guaranteeing P(CS) >= p
nodes.statement: Our goal is to find the minimal $N$ which ensures correct selection of all of the required $s$ populations with probability of at least $p\in(0,1)$ for this procedure.

nodes.name: P(CS) cannot be controlled without further assumptions
nodes.statement: It is not possible to control the probability of correct selection (denoted by $\mathbb{P}(CS)$) without further assumptions.
conclusions: It is not possible to control the probability of correct selection (denoted by $\mathbb{P}(CS)$) without further assumptions.

nodes.name: Equal-means counterexample
nodes.statement: To see this, take populations with equal means, $\theta_{\gamma} := \gamma \cdot \textbf{1}_k;\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$. There is no way to distinguish between the populations by sampling from them and the $\mathbb{P}(CS)$ is not sensitive to $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample: with all means equal the populations are indistinguishable and P(CS) does not depend on N.

nodes.name: Indifference-zone parameter space Theta(Delta,k)
nodes.statement: In order to allow the user to distinguish between populations, the indifference-zone approach of Bechhofer \cite{bechhofer1954single} is adopted, i.e. the parameter-space is restricted in the following way \begin{equation} \theta \in \Theta(\Delta,k) := \{\tilde{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^k;\tilde{\theta}_{[k-s+1]}-\tilde{\theta}_{[k-s]}\geq\Delta\} \end{equation} where $\tilde{\theta}_{[1]}\leq\ldots\leq\tilde{\theta}_{[k]}$ are the ordered means and $\Delta>0$ is a known parameter indicating the minimal difference in mean between the top $s$ and bottom $k-s$ populations.
nodes.statement_short: Bechhofer's indifference zone: means whose top-$s$ and bottom-$(k-s)$ groups are separated by at least $\Delta$.

nodes.name: Indifference-zone parameter space
nodes.statement: \theta \in \Theta(\Delta,k) := \{\tilde{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^k;\tilde{\theta}_{[k-s+1]}-\tilde{\theta}_{[k-s]}\geq\Delta\}
nodes.label: eq:indifference_parameter_space

nodes.name: Delta as the experimenter's indifference level
nodes.statement: $\Delta$ can also be interpreted as the indifference level of the experimenter, i.e. if the absolute value of the difference between the means of two different population is less than $\Delta$, the experimenter will consider them as equivalent populations.

nodes.name: P(CS) tends to 1 as N grows
nodes.statement: Since $(\bar{X}_1,\ldots,\bar{X}_k)$ is a consistent estimator for any $\theta\in\Theta(\Delta,k)$, the probability of correct selection tends to $1$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$, regardless of the true parametrization.
assumptions: $(\bar{X}_1,\ldots,\bar{X}_k)$ is a consistent estimator for any $\theta\in\Theta(\Delta,k)$
conclusions: the probability of correct selection tends to $1$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$, regardless of the true parametrization

nodes.name: The minimal sample size is well-defined
nodes.statement: Thus, the minimal sample size which ensures correct selection with probability $p$ is well-defined.
conclusions: the minimal sample size which ensures correct selection with probability $p$ is well-defined

nodes.name: Minimal sample size N*_{k,s}(p)
nodes.statement: Fix $\Delta>0$ and denote by $N^*_{k,s}(p)$ the minimal $N\in\mathbb{N}$ for which the probability of correct selection is above $p$.

nodes.name: N*_{k,s}(p) as solution of P(CS)=p, event CS^s_{k,N}
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we follow \cite{gupta2002multiple} and ignore the rounding error, i.e. $N_{k,s}^*(p)$ is defined as the solution of the following equation \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}(CS_{k,N_{k,s}^*}^s;\Delta,\theta^*)=p \end{equation} where $CS_{k,N}^s$ is the event of making correct selection of the $s$ out of $k$ populations with the highest means based on $N$ samples from each population.
nodes.statement_short: Ignoring rounding, $N^*_{k,s}(p)$ solves $P(CS^s_{k,N};\Delta,\theta^*)=p$, $CS^s_{k,N}$ being correct selection of the top $s$ with $N$ samples each.

nodes.name: Defining equation of N*_{k,s}(p)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}(CS_{k,N_{k,s}^*}^s;\Delta,\theta^*)=p
nodes.label: eq:h_1_integral

nodes.name: Least favorable configuration (LFC)
nodes.statement: In addition, $\theta^*$ is some \textit{least favorable configuration (LFC)}, i.e. it is a parametrization which satisfies \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}(CS^s_{k,N_{k,s}};\Delta, \theta^*)=\inf_{\tilde{\theta}\in\Theta(\Delta,k)}\mathbb{P}(CS^s_{k,N_{k,s}};\Delta,\tilde{\theta})\ \ . \end{equation}

nodes.name: LFC attains the infimum of P(CS)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{P}(CS^s_{k,N_{k,s}};\Delta, \theta^*)=\inf_{\tilde{\theta}\in\Theta(\Delta,k)}\mathbb{P}(CS^s_{k,N_{k,s}};\Delta,\tilde{\theta})\ \ .

nodes.name: Robbins-Siegmund asymptotic sample size
nodes.statement: With regard to this model, it was shown in \cite{robbins1967iterated} that for $s=1$ and $k\rightarrow\infty$, $N_{k,s=1}^*(p)\sim\frac{2\sigma^2}{\Delta^2}\ln(k-1)$ regardless of the value of $p\in(0,1)$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence a_k ~ b_k
nodes.statement: The asymptotic notation $\sim$ is interpreted in its classical terminology, i.e. for any two sequences $a_k\sim b_k$ if and only if $\frac{a_k}{b_k} \overset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 1$.

nodes.name: Selection-size regime s_k -> s-bar, ln(s_k)/ln(k-s_k) -> C
nodes.statement: We study the more general settings where the inequality $1\leq s:=s_k<k-s_k$ holds asymptotically and both limits $s_k\rightarrow\bar{s}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ and $\frac{\ln(s_k)}{\ln(k-s_k)}\rightarrow C\in[0,1]$ exist (e.g. $s_k\equiv \bar{s}\in\mathbb{N}$, $s_k:=\ln(k)$ and $s_k:=\psi k^{\beta}; 0<\psi,0<\beta \leq 1$ with $\psi<\frac{1}{2}$ for $\beta=1$).
nodes.statement_short: Regime: $1\le s_k<k-s_k$, $s_k\to\bar s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ and $\ln s_k/\ln(k-s_k)\to C\in[0,1]$ (e.g. $s_k$ fixed, $\ln k$, $\psi k^\beta$).

nodes.name: Shorthand N*_k(p)
nodes.statement: To simplify notation, let $N^*_k(p):=N^*_{s_k,k}(p)$ when $s_k$ is understood from context.

nodes.name: ln(k-s_k) may be replaced by ln(k)
nodes.statement: Observe that in the following statement we can replace $\ln(k-s_k)$ by $\ln(k)$ in the asymptotic expression $\tilde{N}_k^*$ because the assumption that asymptotically $1\leq s_k\leq\frac{k}{2}$ implies $\ln(k-s_k)\sim\ln(k)$.

nodes.name: Generalized Robbins-Siegmund theorem
nodes.statement: Let $s_k$ be a sequence such that: (i) $\forall k\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\leq s_k\leq k-s_k$. (ii) $s_k\rightarrow\bar{s}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$, and (iii) $\frac{\ln(s_k)}{\ln(k-s_k)}\rightarrow C\in[0,1]$. Then, $\forall p\in(0,1)$ the following statements hold: \begin{enumerate} \item There exists $K_p\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $N^*_k(p)$ exists for any $k>K_p$. \item $N^*_k(p) \sim \tilde{N}_k^* := \frac{2\sigma^2(1+\sqrt{C})^2}{\Delta^2}\ln(k-s_k)$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: There exists $K_p\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $N^*_k(p)$ exists for any $k>K_p$.
nodes.statement_short: For every $p$, $N^*_k(p)$ eventually exists and $N^*_k(p)\sim 2\sigma^2(1+\sqrt C)^2\ln(k-s_k)/\Delta^2$, independent of $p$ to first order.
nodes.label: thm:generalized_sigmound_robbins

nodes.name: Dudewicz and Dalal's two-stage procedure P_E
nodes.statement: \caption{Dudewicz and Dalal\:'s Two-Stage Procedure $P_E$} \justify {\bf Input:} $\Delta$ - indifference parameter, $N_0 \geq 2$ - initial sample size, $p$ - desired $\mathbb{P}(CS)$ \\ {\bf Output:} $\hat{i}$ - selected population \\ {\bf Stage One:} \begin{enumerate} \item Draw $N_0$ observations from each population $\Pi_i;i=1,\ldots,k+1$ \item Compute the casual unbiased estimate $S^2_i$ for $\sigma^2_i$ from the initial sample taken for each $\Pi_i$ \end{enumerate} {\bf Stage Two:} \begin{enumerate} \item For each $i=1,\ldots,k+1$ draw $N_i-N_0$ more samples from $\Pi_i$, where $N_i$ is given by \begin{equation} N_i=\max\bigg\{N_0+1,\bigg \lceil \bigg(\frac{h_k^{(1)}}{\Delta}\bigg)^2 S_i^2\bigg\rceil \bigg\} . \end{equation} Here $\lceil y \rceil$ denotes the smallest integer which is $\geq y$, and the constant $h_k^{(1)}$ is specified in eq. \eqref{eq:h1_integral_def}. \item Select numbers $\{a_{ij};j=1,\ldots,N_i\}_{i=1}^{k+1}$ such that $\forall i=1,\ldots,k+1$: \begin{enumerate} \item $S^2_i\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}a_{ij}^2=\bigg(\frac{\Delta}{h_k^{(1)}}\bigg)^2$ \item $\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}a_{ij}=1$ \item $a_{i1}=\ldots=a_{iN_0}$ \end{enumerate} \item Select the population $\hat{i}$ by the rule \begin{equation} \hat{i} := \underset{i=1,\ldots,k+1}{\arg\max} \big\{\sum_{j=1}^{N_i} a_{ij} X_{ij};\big\} \end{equation} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Stage one estimates each variance from $N_0$ samples; stage two tops up to $N_i\propto S_i^2(h/\Delta)^2$ samples and selects the largest weighted mean.
nodes.label: alg:dudewicz_dalal

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement: \proof \begin{enumerate} \item To derive the asymptotics of $h_k^{(2)}(\infty)$, recall that a standard Student's $t$-distribution with $\nu=\infty$ d.f's is a standard Gaussian distribution. Thus, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots\stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,2)$ and observe that \begin{equation} f_2(h,k):=\mathbb{P} \Big(\max_{j=1,\ldots,k} X_j\leq h\Big)=\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{j=1,\ldots,k}Z_j\leq\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\Big) \end{equation} where $Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,1)$. As mentioned in Section \ref{sec:robbins_siegmund}, the normalizing constants of the standard Gaussian distribution are $a_k=\sqrt{2\ln(k)}$ and $b_k\sim\sqrt{2\ln(k)}$. Thus, for any $\tau\in(0,p\wedge 1-p)$ define $h_k(\tau)^+:=\sqrt{2}(b_k-\frac{g_{p\pm\tau}}{a_k})$ where $g_{p\pm\tau}$ is the $p \pm\tau$'s quantile of the standard Gumbel distribution. Since the extreme value distribution of the standard Gaussian distribution is a standard Gumbel distribution, this implies that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty} f_2 \big(h_k^{\pm}(\tau),k\big)=p\pm\tau . \end{equation} Therefore, by the same technique which was used in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:dalal_asymptotic}, deduce that $h_k^{(2)}(\infty) \sim \sqrt{2}(b_k-\frac{q_p}{a_k})\sim\sqrt{2}b_k \sim 2 \sqrt{\ln(k)}$. \item To derive the asymptotics of $h_k^{(1)}$, set an arbitrary $\tau\in{(0,p\wedge 1-p)}$ and define $h_k^\pm(\tau)=b_k-z_{p\pm\tau}$ where $z_p$ is the $p$'th quantile of the standard Gaussian distribution. Let $Z_1,Z_2,\ldots \stackrel{i.i.d}{\sim}N(0,1)$. For \begin{equation} f_1(h,k):=\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{j=1,\ldots,k} Z_j+Z_{k+1}\leq h\Big) \end{equation} Theorem \ref{thm:sum_max_a_k_positive} implies that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}f\big(h_k^\pm(\tau),k\big)=p\pm\tau . \end{equation} Thus, the same technique used to prove Theorem \ref{thm:dalal_asymptotic} shows that $h_k^{(1)}(\infty) \sim b_k \sim \sqrt{2\ln(k)}$. \end{enumerate} \endproof

nodes.statement: It is instructive to compare Theorem \ref{thm:optimal_asymptotic} in the case of equal variances $\sigma_i \equiv \sigma$ to Robbins and Siegmund\:'s one-stage procedure applied when the variance is known.
